stem: Why should a website store a salted hash of each password instead of the password itself?

options.text: If the database leaks, the passwords are not directly readable
A hash can be turned back into the password whenever the user forgets it
options.why: Hashing is one-way; that is the point. Resetting a password is the right recovery path.

options.text: Hashing makes the login page load faster
options.why: Hashing adds a little work; it is done for security, not speed.

options.text: Hashed passwords never need to be changed
options.why: Users should still change a password they suspect is exposed.

explain: A salted hash cannot be reversed into the password, and the unique salt stops attackers reusing one precomputed table against every account. A leaked database then gives them much less than a list of plain passwords.

stem: Which TWO choices make a password harder to guess?

options.text: Using the same password on every site
options.why: Reuse means one breach exposes all your accounts.

options.text: Using a different password for each site
Basing it on your pet's name
options.why: Personal details are among the first things an attacker tries.

explain: Length and uniqueness matter most. Reuse and personal details make guessing and credential stuffing easy. A password manager makes long, unique passwords practical.

stem: An attacker steals a list of leaked passwords from one site and tries them on many other sites. What is this attack called?

options.why: Phishing tricks a person into giving up a password; it does not replay a leaked list.
That is watching someone type; no leaked list is involved.
That is following someone through a physical door.

explain: Credential stuffing replays leaked username and password pairs against other services, and it works because people reuse passwords. Unique passwords per site defeat it.

options.text: It needs two or more different kinds of proof, such as a password and a code from your phone
It asks for a long password
options.why: One long password is still a single factor (something you know).

options.text: It asks for the password twice
options.why: Two entries of the same factor are still one factor.

options.text: It locks the account after three wrong tries
options.why: Lockout limits guessing but is not a second factor.

explain: The factors are something you know, something you have and something you are. Multi-factor combines different kinds, so stealing a password alone is not enough.
references: NIST SP 800-63B, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Lifecycle Management

stem: A code generated by an authenticator app on your phone is which kind of factor?

options.why: A password or PIN is something you know; the code comes from your device.
That is a fingerprint, face or similar trait.
That is a location factor, not a code from an app.

explain: The code proves you hold the enrolled device, so it is something you have. Pair it with a password (something you know) for two different factors.

stem: Which TWO pairs count as multi-factor authentication?

options.why: Both are something you know, so this is one factor used twice.
Two passwords are still the same kind of factor.

explain: Each correct pair mixes two different kinds: know plus are, and have plus know. Two things from the same kind are not multi-factor.
